You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 31
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 78

# The Weight of an Unanswered Call

Linh is a 31-year-old Vietnamese-Australian journalist who, until two years ago, described her life as one built on momentum — deadlines met, stories filed, always moving forward. That momentum collapsed on a Tuesday morning when her younger brother, Minh, was killed in a hit-and-run accident while cycling to work. He was 27. Linh learned about his death not from family, but from a missed call notification followed by a text from her mother that she still cannot bring herself to delete from her phone.

She had been on assignment that morning, interviewing a local councillor about urban infrastructure — a story she now finds grotesque in its irony, given that Minh died on a poorly lit stretch of road the city had been promising to improve for years. She remembers finishing the interview, checking her phone in the car park, and reading her mother's words on a cracked screen. She sat in her car for four hours before she could drive. She does not remember those four hours at all.

In the weeks that followed, Linh moved through the rituals of grief — the Buddhist funeral rites, the white mourning clothes, the relatives crowding her parents' home in Footscray. She returned to work within ten days because, she says, sitting still felt like drowning. Her editors praised her resilience. She accepted the praise and said nothing about the fact that she had been sleeping on her couch because she could not tolerate the silence of her bedroom, or that she had stopped eating anything that required preparation because Minh used to call her every Sunday while she cooked.

Her marriage, already strained, did not survive the year. Her ex-husband describes her as having become "unreachable," and she does not dispute this. She simply stopped being able to explain to him — or to herself — why she flinched at the sound of bicycle bells, why she could not watch the evening news without her chest seizing, why she sometimes pulled her car to the side of the road and sat gripping the steering wheel, certain she was about to die.

Linh is still working. She is, by most external measures, professionally accomplished — she was recently shortlisted for a regional journalism award. But the work has changed in texture. She gravitates toward stories about institutional failure and preventable deaths, filing them with a precision her colleagues admire and she experiences as compulsion. She cannot stop. She believes, in a way she has never articulated to anyone, that if she documents enough preventable tragedies, something will eventually make sense about Minh's.

She rarely sleeps more than three hours consecutively. When she does sleep, she dreams of her phone screen — the cracked glass, the notification light blinking — and wakes with her heart hammering, reaching for Minh's contact in her phone before she is fully conscious. She has not deleted his number. She has called it twice, both times at 2 a.m., listening to his voicemail greeting until the line disconnected.

She describes herself as permanently braced — as though the world has revealed itself to be the kind of place where the worst thing can happen on any ordinary Tuesday, and she must now live accordingly. She scans intersections when she drives. She tracks the whereabouts of her parents and her closest friend with an anxiety she recognizes as excessive and cannot modulate. At family gatherings, she positions herself near exits and finds reasons to leave early.

What she finds most difficult to explain is not the grief itself — she understands grief, has written about it — but the way time has stopped organizing itself properly. Minh's death does not feel like something that happened two years ago. It feels like something that is always, in some register, still happening. The Tuesday morning with the cracked phone screen exists in the same continuous present as every moment since, and she does not yet know how to live in a time that has moved on without her consent.
